An explosive Lanterns still stays stubbornly grounded in character

Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre's prickly chemistry continues to outshine Lanterns' superheroics.

By Dennis Perkins  |  September 6, 2026 | 10:00pm
Photo: John Johnson/HBO Max
TV Reviews Lanterns
Copy to clipboard
  • Copy Link
  • Facebook

Sponsored by

Instaread

At the halfway point in Lanterns’ first season, it’s time to accept the series for what it is—and what has chosen not to be.

This week, no greater comics authority than Grant Morrison* chimed in on Lanterns, offering up a mixed but leaning-positive review of this deliberately low-key superhero tale. Morrison, lured to watch by their annoyance over statements from co-creator Damon Lindelof seemingly mocking the sort of slam-bang comic book elements that—let’s face it—many fans were hoping for, nonetheless had copious praise for Aaron Pierre and (especially) Kyle Chandler. (Even if they confessed that Chandler’s Hal, whom Morrison calls “Dr. McCoy,” “wasn’t any Hal Jordan [they] recognized.”

Morrison’s main complaint, one shared by a moderate swath of the fan community, is a fundamental and structural one. Why turn Green Lantern—on of DC’s most high-flying, cosmically scaled comics universes—into a decidedly Earth-bound, occasionally dour, effects-skimpy street-level TV series? As Morrison states, “DC has a ton of ‘ground level’ heroes, or characters with low-level gimmick powers to choose from, so why take this low-fi route with a franchise that should be competing with Star Trek or Star Wars?”

It’s a question that’s been running through the series’ first three episodes, where ring-slinging is sparse and Chandler’s Jordan is portrayed as someone who’s been soaking in the adulation from his flashy, costumed heroics so long that he’s a little embarrassed by it. The scene where John dutifully fetches Hal’s Lantern only for Hal to see one of his long-mothballed Green Lantern suits packed in the same duffel bag gets at the central conflict ably. John, literally raised to be a Green Lantern, wants to get to the good stuff already, while the current keeper of the flame shies away from shining it on evildoers—or, indeed, at all.

John, as Marine-straight and patiently impatient as he looms in Hal’s periphery, wants that ring—and that suit. His desire to help people is the one link he shares with his unwilling mentor, that unspoken tie holding John back from doing what Laura Linney’s Guardian grows more insistent each episode that he do and just taking the ring off of Hal Jordan’s finger.

“The Weenie,” from its jokey title on down, tilts as close as Lanterns has gotten yet to the buddy-cop element overrepresented in the promotional materials. (If not to the cosmic action or, as John mocking calls out Hal’s wonted strategy, “fly[ing] in with green fists.”) Hal, having broken into William Macon’s high-tech storage facility, displays some old school action-comedy timing as he—stepping on a hidden pressure plate—asks John warily, “Did you just hear a click?” He also straight up teases John for making a legit joke as they surveil Macon’s ranch before their mission. Hal also makes the requisite joke to Kerry about John “finding Macon’s weenie.” (“Weenie” being the architectural term for an eye-catching architectural feature designed to draw attention, as the artistically minded John explains.)

But “The Weenie” slyly undercuts all this apparent thawing between John and Hal by revealing just how carefully each of them is calculating their next moves under cover of the snatches of banter. The episode kicks off in space (or a budget-friendly isolation cell therein), where Ulrich Thomsen’s Sinestro plays Hannibal Lecter-style mind games with the uneasily suited-up Hal.

Thomsen (as he showed with Banshee’s icily human crime lord Kai Proctor) is exquisitely measured in his villainy. After teasing that the Manhunter hiding in Rushville is “the second greatest threat” Hal’s currently facing, Sinestro makes Hal admit that John is the first, Hal finally saying out loud that he knows full well that the younger, more straitlaced Stewart is his replacement. Sinestro sees easily through Hal’s attempts at bluster, as Hal calls him “Johnny Tryhard” and pronounces him “boring.”

Sinestro, imprisoned for betraying his oath by taking the Guardians’ quest for order to its predictably fascistic extremes, rebuts Hal’s defensive claim that he, unlike his mentor, isn’t evil. Thomsen’s offhand answer, “I was never anything but myself” is yet another telling ding in the all-knowing Guardians’ reputation, and Chandler makes Hal’s growing unease register on his inadequately shielded expression.

The episode, apart from John and Hal’s abortive raid on Macon’s compound (they’re overcome by some high-tech blackout weapons that negate Hal’s ring), is all hushed conversations like this. Linney’s Guardian manipulates John (much more bluntly than the subtle Sinestro), by revealing that Hal had “violated his oath” by visiting his disgraced mentor and then insulting John and his parents until John takes the bait. (“I did not realize your father’s weakness runs within you,” is especially cold.)

John initially bucks at the Guardians’ unanimous decision that Hal’s actions have “accelerated the inevitable,” and that John should now simply take the ring from him. Another bluntly wielded revelation that Hal told the Guardians John, “lacks creativity” and  “is too weak to bear the massive power of the ring” seemingly does the trick, as a visibly pissed off John tells his visitor Hal “didn’t do shit to earn it” and was merely keeping it warm until he showed up.

John’s words are echoed back at just the wrong time later when, after they track down the supposed owner of a killer satellite that zaps Zoe’s pickup truck to smithereens (we’ll get there), John’s words are played back in incriminating snippets. On their way (driving) to their target’s high-tech slaughterhouse headquarters (never a good sign), John and Hal had bonded, sincerely, it seems, about the risks and sacrifices they’ve both endured in their careers doing what they thought was right. Hal, trying to console the stoic John about Zoe’s sudden demise, notes somberly, “People dying is part of the job…Avoid real relationships from here on out. Keep people at a distance for their own safety. Lonely fuckin’ job…”

And so when Hal brushes off John’s recorded betrayal by nimbly trapping a deceptive interviewee (Jason Manuel Olazábal as Hector Hammond) with Homicide-level interrogation techniques (and a little 24-style threatening), we’re primed to accept this more softened Hal. Until their drive back to Rushville turns out to have been an expert gambit by Hal to get John to confess not just that he’s been tasked to take the ring (which, John notes, he did not do at the ranch when he had the chance) but also that he thinks Zoe is alive—and the Manhunter.

Both Chandler and Pierre are exceptional here, each laying down a card at a time until Hal’s revealed to be holding the kicker. After getting John to call Antaan and the alien hit squad for a meet-up, Hal accepts John’s apology for the things he’d said. Then grinning, “And I’m sorry about the rental,” Hal pulls the series’ second dive out of a moving car and, with no ring to save him, passenger John is left to smash into a waiting telephone pole.

This, then, is the nature of Lanterns’ action. The laser beam effectively seems to kill off a major character, but the fireworks (and Hal’s resulting green protective bubble over the motel) are subservient to the Hal and John dynamic. (“Where’d it come from?,” Hal barks, emerging from his room, and when John replies with coordinates, Hal’s snapped, “Just fuckin’ point!,” sees him fly off and retrieve the destroyed satellite.) The raid on Macon’s compound has John’s nifty digger and some so-so CGI weaponry, but it’s the wary camaraderie between Chandler and Pierre that we care about. The car crash finale gag could come out of a Smokey And The Bandit movie (Hal’s shit-eating grin and all), but the wounds on both sides lingering after Hal and John’s confrontation echo louder than the smash.

As Morrison complained, this approach does seem antithetical to the Green Lantern vibe. But it is a considered choice to ground (in all senses) this latest outpost in the suddenly shaky James Gunn DCU in character over spectacle, and with such strong performers (Kerry Macdonald making a co-equal third in the series’ leading trio), the incongruity is working. It might not be what people expected, but Lanterns continues to be its own, admirably singular thing.

Stray observations

  • • *Grant Morrison being the greatest comics writer alive today, and no, I will not be taking any questions. 
  • • Thomson makes Sinestro’s manipulation of the insecure Hal look so easy. His initial pitch to just murder Stewart rebuffed (as he no doubt anticipated), he dangles just enough insider Manhunter knowledge to convince Hal that he’s necessary—and that Hal can use his triumph to kill John’s favor with their bosses instead.
  • • Manhunters have a crystal heart which is the only thing that they can’t disguise. Let the disemboweling knives be sharpened.
  • • Hal, swooping in to ruin John’s water tower surveillance, puts on his best flyboy front as he excuses his absence by telling John he was “getting laid in space.”
  • • Hal ensures John won’t accept a ring-aided ride by offering up the choice, “Well, I can either carry you like a baby or you can hop on, pretend I’m a horse.”
  • • Not enough is made of Aaron Pierre’s cagy work as John navigates not just the cosmic elements of his predicament, but also his confident code-switching in an all-white American small town. The gun shop scene, where John plasters on a bulletproof friendliness in the face of some locals’ hostility, not only sees him get the sniper scope he wanted (he leaves the rifle he was forced to buy with a roll of cash on the counter), but also a dodgy sandwich for his troubles.
  • • Explaining the shape-shifting Manhunters to Kerry, John says, “they’re not aliens, they’re something else.” For those needing a refresher, Jarrod Jones has you covered.
  • • As with the current comics iteration of John Stewart, John’s digging machine is carefully thought-out, designed, and executed to the smallest green rivet. Lacks imagination, indeed.
  • • I will note the change from the comics where the ring can only be used by the one its chosen, although the fact that the Guardians have deemed John worthy does make it plausible that Hal’s ring would work for him, too. Still, it’s a lot more loosey-goosey here than in established lore.
  • • Plus, the militia’s “darkness guns” nullifying Hal’s ring seems to indicate that the whole “weakness to yellow” thing is out the window.
  • • Kerry makes the save when John and Hal are captured, defying her father-in-law and irrevocably throwing her lot in with the interloping heroes. A fact she uses to cow the glib Hal into silence once she drops them sheepishly back at their motel.
  • • So Zoe’s the Manhunter, right? Can’t say I would be shocked–the law of extraneous characters aside, she tells John she healed William, which he had previously attributed to his “benefactor.” And here’s to Poorna Jagannathan getting more to do. 
  • • Okay, first, props to Garrett Dillahunt’s workout regimen. But did anyone else get a William Fichtner in Go vibe from his startling one-upmanship in demanding John draw him in his office (and in the nude)?
  • • The sterile, cow-dismembering laser room in Hammond’s slaughterhouse is very Severance. As Hal notes about the ambience, “Jazz… that can’t be good.”

Star Trek: Strange New Worlds goes full soap opera, to mixed results

“Like Chronitons Through The Hourglass,” so are the days of the Enterprise.

By Caroline Siede  |  September 3, 2026 | 9:00am
Photo: Christos Kalohoridis/Paramount+
TV Reviews Star Trek: Strange New Worlds
Copy to clipboard
  • Copy Link
  • Facebook
  • X
  • Reddit
  • Bluesky
130

When you commit to a long-term relationship with a TV show, you have to learn to see it for what it is and not what you want it to be. My ideal version of Star Trek isn’t a show driven by weekly pastiches of various genres. But it’s clear that, at least this far into its run, that is primarily what Strange New Worlds wants to be. This season alone has delivered a haunted -house thriller, a stoner comedy, a film noir, a Mpuppet episode, and a real-time disaster movie riff, with only the premiere as an episode that isn’t fundamentally built around a genre homage (and even that one had dinosaurs in it). Now this week’s installment adds “soap- opera parody” to the list. Rather than critique that overall structural choice, however, it feels more productive to dig into how these homages are and aren’t working to serve a Star Trek-ian ethos.

On an intellectual level, “Like Chronitons Through The Hourglass” is maybe the most interesting genre riff we’ve gotten yet, if only because it’s the first episode of the season to openly acknowledge it’s doing a genre riff. Pike wakes up from a “shuttle accident” shocked to discover he’s now in a melodramatic version of the Enterprise where the lighting is bright and hazy and the dramatic pauses are extended. Instead of just accepting his new reality, however, he calls out its strangeness and starts looking for an explanation. It turns out Rhys Darby’s “fancy coat god guy” is back after his last appearance in “Wedding Bell Blues” and he’s purposefully put the crew into a soap -opera world as part of an experiment for his dissertation on the human race.   

The fact that there’s a reason for this to be happening makes it more palatable than something like “A Case Of Chiaroscuro,” where it was actively distracting that the crew never acknowledged they’d stumbled upon a Klingon version of 1940s Earth. Technically, Strange New Worlds still hasn’t confirmed that Darby is Original Series player Trelane and that Trelane is part of the Q Continuum, but that’s certainly the implication here. And there’s a long, proud history of Q characters messing with Starfleet crews for misguided but at least kind of well-meaning ends. After emotionally torturing the crew out of pettiness and spite last time, now he wants to help them access “the raw unrepentant beauty of human emotion” via soap -opera mechanics. The show even brings on real-life Days Of Our Lives star Deidre Hall as the ship’s counselor to drive home the idea that “the search for emotional truth and scientific truth are the same, you just have to want to see it.”

The trouble is, the actual execution of the soap- opera premise just isn’t all that engaging. The joke is that being trapped in a soap -opera world forces the crew to discuss their feelings in a way they usually avoid. Except other than a few extra camera zooms, the writing itself isn’t all that different from how this show usually feels week to week. While Trelane asserts that “space adventures leave little time for humans to deal with their inner struggles,” Strange New Worlds loves to have its characters openly explain what they’re going through, like all that stuff about Chapel having one foot out the door last week. The show’s true challenge is letting its emotional throughlines unfold in a subtle, nuanced way rather than in blunt conversations where characters just state their arcs. In that sense “Like Chronitons Through The Hourglass” is emphasizing a writing problem rather than addressing it. 

There are a few solid laughs here, including Uhura dramatically announcing she’s Pike’s secret daughter and M’Benga’s self-diagnosis of “space madness.” But the way those storylines resolve with characters saying things like “remember who you are and look to your friends” is basically exactly how they would resolve in a non-soap-opera episode too, which means they don’t really land as parody. That’s also why the one subplot that really pops is Ethan Peck playing Spock’s evil brother Sybok, which is a very funny (and dare I say hot?!?) juxtaposition with how he’s usually used on the show. The idea of exploring Spock’s secret inner passion may be familiar territory for Star Trek, but the Sexy Sybok runner at least takes advantage of the soap -opera premise to showcase a steamier energy rather than just discussing that theme in the abstract.  

Yet just as I was ready to write off this episode as another style-over-substance entry, it genuinely surprised me with the reveal that the thing Pike is truly processing this week is the loss of the daughter he remembers raising in the illusion Marie Batel projected for them in last season’s finale. At the time, Strange New Worlds didn’t make that big of a deal about the fact that Pike basically lived through his own version of “The Inner Light.” But that only makes it more poignant to unexpectedly return to it here. He may have made peace with letting go of Marie, but letting go of the future he could have had with her is a whole other matter. 

Given how much Pike’s bittersweet ending in “The Menagerie” hinges on the idea of finding happiness living in an illusion, it’s always fascinating when Strange New Worlds preemptively plays around with those ideas. I’ve long wondered if this show is going to tweak Pike’s Original Series fate in some way and his longing to reunite with his imaginary daughter Juliet (Anna Mirodin) certainly raises one possibility ofon how it might do that. Still, given how moving the Juliet reveal is, I wish we’d gotten to spend more time with her and Pike together rather than rushing through their brief scene in favor of goofy jokes about Spock’s living heart transplant.

In the end, the most compelling thing about “Like Chronitons Through The Hourglass” is a quality it shares with the (much better) horror movie homage from earlier in the season: the lack of clear-cut emotional resolution. For as much as the Spock/La’An relationship has never really worked for me, I was unexpectedly moved by their post-breakup conversation this week. There’s something about her clearly conflicted feelings butting up against his placid demeanor that captures the poignant tragedy of Spock’s relationship with humanity. His simple “I thought our intention was to stay friends” pushes her away, not because he’s trying to but because she’s processing something his logical perspective fundamentally can’t understand. That’s emotional character work explored through something beyond blunt dialogue.

That emotional ambiguity extends to Pike as well, in the moving final scene where he breaks down in his therapy session. Though Anson Mount is the nominal lead of Strange New Worlds, he can feel a bit underserved beyond his wacky comedy chops. “Like Chronitons Through The Hourglass” lets him tackle some weightier material for once, which is a welcome change of pace and a challenge he more than rises to. I’m still not convinced we needed a soap- opera parody to get us to all that. But at least there’s something going on beneath the surface of this week’s requisite genre homage.

Stray observations

  • • Pike hearing the strings of soap- opera scoring and immediately asking “Are we back in a musical?” made me laugh.
  • • So was Uhura actually adopted or was that made-up backstory for the soap -opera world?
  • • Trelane’s teacher is dressed almost exactly like Q in “Encounter At Farpoint,” only with a slightly different headdress.  
  • • La’An argues that logic gives Spock a non-judgmental sense of empathy and grace, which I don’t think feels true of Peck’s portrayal of him but is a great encapsulation of what makes Leonard Nimoy’s performance so good.
  • • On the other hand, watching Peck as Sexy Sybok is the first time I’ve truly felt the fact that he’s Gregory Peck’s grandson. Let’s get him into some romantic dramas after this show wraps up! 
  • • So do we think the random Una/M’Benga romance is actually going to stick? Or will it be like the time “Shuttle To Kenfori” presented him as Pike’s best friend and then the show never returned to that dynamic again? 
  • • No Scotty or Pelia this week, which is a shame because Martin Quinn and Carol Kane both feel like they could crush a soap -opera parody. 
  • • Confession time: I was very conflicted about whether to grade this episode a C+ or a B- and I do think Trelane’s final project grade wound up swaying me. Congrats to the show for pulling an Inception.

Guy Ritchie romp The Gentlemen expands its empire of excess in season 2

A frustrating lack of Daniel Ings notwithstanding, Guy Ritchie's gangster extravaganza returns for another entertaining ride.

By Saloni Gajjar  |  September 3, 2026 | 3:00am
Photo: Christopher Raphael/Netflix
TV Reviews The Gentlemen
Copy to clipboard
  • Copy Link
  • Facebook
  • X
  • Reddit
  • Bluesky
28

The Gentlemen wears its outrageousness proudly. Set in the same universe as Guy Ritchie’s middling 2019 film of the same name, season one of the adrenaline-heavy TV series made for enjoyable viewing.  In every sense of the word: This is an entertaining action romp with vivid production design and striking sets. It’s jam-packed with brutal shootouts and fiery combat that’s a lot of bloody fun and, somehow, hardly monotonous. The impeccably styled characters of its world live in lavish mansions, speak in zippy dialogue, and cherish crude British slang. Season two follows suit but broadens the show’s horizons as criminal partners Eddie Halstead (Theo James) and Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario), who simply can’t seem to sort out their feelings for each other, strive to expand their weed empire to Italy, the Middle East, and South America.

Along the way, the second season crams in violence in the form of beheadings and torture scenes, as well as gun-toting thugs who want to team up with or defeat the duo. Eddie and Susie—who run the operation for her calculating, imprisoned, sauna-loving father, Bobby (Ray Winstone)—find their command of Bobby’s enterprise challenged by rivals, loved ones, and each other. The result is a sufficiently thrilling saga that, in typical Ritchie fashion, comes with plenty of flair and ridiculous caveats. If season one was about former armyman Eddie coming to terms with his surprising Dukedom and inheritance—including a 15,000-acre estate and all the marijuana sales and distribution that came with it—then the second sees him rise to the top of a grisly food chain as he leaves dead bodies and broken hearts in his wake. 

At this point, Eddie is no longer trying to get out of his dead dad’s shady business. Why would he when he’s a surprisingly conniving dude with a knack for schemes, lies, and murder? Does all the brutality take a toll on his soul? In these eight hour-long episodes, The Gentlemen finds answers to these questions that are both absurd yet quite meaningful. There’s a darkly funny church confession; Eddie’s mom, Lady Sabrina (Joely Richardson), fears he’s losing his way; and billionaire Stanley Johnston (Giancarlo Esposito) infrequently drops in to talk about Jesus and power. But this isn’t a show about contemplation—it’s not a gritty mob drama like Netflix counterparts Peaky Blinders and Ozark. 

On the contrary, The Gentlemen has a revolving door of ludicrous gangsters who burst into Eddie and Susie’s lives and usually don’t exit with their own. Season two brings back some familiar faces (including an all-too-brief visit by Guz Khan as the money launderer Chucky), along with new ones who test the pair. One episode focuses almost entirely on Eddie and Susie hunting down a rare falcon to help Eddie gain a huge political favor, leading to knowingly convoluted lines like, “Without that bird, we will be short 26 votes, our attempts to Shanghai the House of the Lords will fail, and I’ll be on the hook for $60 million to an Italian crime boss.”  

Said Italian crime boss is Marco Moretti (Sergio Castelitto), who, along with his beloved goddaughter Bella (Benedetta Porcaroli) and bumbling henchman Cico (Michele Morrone), partners with the protagonists for season two. And wouldn’t you know it, Eddie and Bella are a match made in criminal heaven. The show hastily depicts their romance, one driven partly by mutual attraction and partly by business prudence. However, by rushing through their courtship, The Gentlemen does its own expansive plot quite a disservice—in such a rush, their love just doesn’t seem believable. 

It also robs us of the sizzling chemistry that James and Scodelario coolly crafted in season one. Instead of allowing their banter to simmer to a boiling point, the middle portions of season two keep them apart for disappointingly long stretches of time. Neither Eddie nor Susie are particularly expressive because of the nature of their job, but being relatively stoic doesn’t limit both actors from conveying their characters’ innermost desires. So whenever James and Scodelario share the screen, The Gentlemen truly comes alive. (Also a letdown: The meager amount of attention paid to the other significant relationship in Eddie’s life: A rehab plot for his brother Freddie keeps season-one scene-stealer Daniel Ings largely out of commission.)

Other changes, including a more serialized approach compared to season one, don’t exactly weigh down The Gentlemen. That’s because Ritchie continues to skillfully infuse the episodic format with his signature style—jokey onscreen text and narrations, snarky interactions, slow-motion shots, etc. That includes neatly executed chase sequences and a stellar Vinnie Jones as Eddie’s suave sidekick—both aspects shine in the heart-pounding, Nick Rowland-directed penultimate episode. The Gentlemen succeeds by not taking itself seriously, as evidenced by, what else, an outrageous and bloody final scene that makes an intriguing setup for a third season. 

Saloni Gajar is The A.V. Club‘s TV critic.

The Gentlemen premieres September 3 on Netflix.

The Shards attempts an episode of vignettes and fails miserably

Even viewers who are suckers for structural experiments will find the penultimate installment more confusing than compelling.

By Ben Rosenstock  |  September 2, 2026 | 10:00pm
(Photo: FX)
TV Reviews the shards
Copy to clipboard
  • Copy Link
  • Facebook
  • X
  • Reddit
  • Bluesky
19

The penultimate episode of The Shards—let us pray that it really is the penultimate episode of the series, not just the season—actually contains a number of storytelling gimmicks that I enjoy. First up: a high school English class where the material and discourse directly pertains to whatever is happening with the characters. That trope can be corny, but also pretty fun when the parallels are real (but not too direct to the point of plagiarism). Most teenagers go to class, and most teenagers make everything about themselves, so it makes sense that discussing a classic novel might bring out personal struggles in their own lives.

In addition to all that, “Hamlet” is an episode broken into three sequential vignettes, each tackling a different ongoing storyline, a structure that often yields a refreshingly different-feeling episode. (The first one that comes to mind for me right now is “The Night Gallery” from season five of Riverdale, since that show had some tonal similarities to this one but occasionally accomplished what it was going for.) Sometimes just concentrating on one story at a time allows for more momentum to build, and more real progress.

So far so good, right? The problem, to put it succinctly, is that pretty much all of the vignettes in “Hamlet” suck. For one, the setup is strange to begin with. The episode begins by rushing through the aftermath of last week: Rhonda recanted what she said about Susan, then got sent to a loony bin in Tennessee. You’d think that her getting abducted and tortured by a serial killer then released would make her a compelling case and someone worth speaking to more, but she’s completely gone from the story now, I guess. You’d also think that Susan might actually enjoy the chance to let loose and be someone other than the perfect queen bee, like she keeps complaining about—but so much for that. Oh, and Debbie is almost entirely missing from this episode, which feels especially weird at this juncture. Again, this is the penultimate episode of the season, right?

At least Matt’s proven death has people talking more, and the police are more motivated to investigate the Trawler than they were before, especially among the student body at Buckley. On the other hand, a large portion of this episode either ignores that central conflict or fails to explore it in a meaningful way. Since the episode is structured in vignettes, it only makes sense to tackle them individually from here.

Romeo And Juliet

Here’s the thing: Susan and Thom will always be each other’s first love, but Susan has fully fallen out of love with Thom. No matter whether Robert was the cause or not, she got the ick for her boyfriend, and we can see it on her face throughout this segment, during every debate with Thom about the validity of Romeo and Juliet’s early-teens love.

The parallels here are, of course, incredibly on the nose to the point of tedium. When the argument relocates to Hamburger Hamlet, Susan claims that Romeo and Juliet were just a “Verona thing” and that both would move on from each other when they left Verona; she’s really saying that she and Thom are meant to move on from each other after high school, but you don’t need me to tell you that. The episode even adds a silly stylistic touch of both characters briefly wearing Elizabethan clothing and directly quoting the play in ways that barely apply to their own situation.

It’s good to see Susan unequivocally break up with Thom, but it has taken so long to get to this point. There was never all that much dramatic juice to this story when Susan barely dealt with any internal conflict about her wavering feelings, and when it seems so easy for her to cut things off now. Additionally, Thom’s sudden suicide pact idea comes out of nowhere, only set up by that one Bruce scene on the bleachers. There’s no real sense of suspense or emotional logic here besides the same old abandonment issues.

Macbeth

Truly, what the hell is this? The lesson is all about revenge and the cycle of violence, but the parallel story is just Steven blackmailing Liz, forcing her to participate in his planned film adaptation of Bret’s Less Than Zero in exchange for holding onto the negatives of her porno movie with Ryan. (Remember Ryan? Hope he enjoyed homecoming court last week.) The Romeo And Juliet parallel was surface-level but at least made some sense in a teen-logic sort of way. Here, there’s barely any connection.

Even setting that aside, who cares about any of this? Sure, Steven hits the nail on the head in realizing that Liz is still holding onto her acting dreams. But we already knew that. This idea of Terry, Liz, and Steven partnering up to make Bret’s movie hasn’t been set up adequately, and coming at this point in the season, it only feels like setup for a potential season two. Again, please let that not happen.

Hamlet

This one actually takes up the most time in the episode, not to mention earning the episode title itself. And thank god for that, because it’s by far the most relevant to, you know, the actual plot of the show. Bret actually is quite like the character of Hamlet in a lot of ways, especially the paranoia and indecision and encroaching madness. I like when both the show and book lean into his unreliable-narrator qualities.

But this vignette is only a marginal improvement on the last two. For one, there’s the scene of Terry sexually assaulting Bret, which gets described in graphic voiceover but feels more abstract than real. I appreciate Bret noting that he thought of this as his choice in the moment, but there’s otherwise no follow-up to this very real trauma, and it’s hard to even contextualize it given that we only see it when he finds the Trawler’s blackmail tape.

Who is the Trawler? Despite having read the book, I have no idea how the show will answer that question. Maybe it’s Robert, the main suspect; Bret’s meeting with Abigail seems to give both him and us plenty more reason to think he’s violent. Maybe it’s Steven, who points out this week that monsters became that way for a reason. Maybe it’s Thom, recently indoctrinated by a cult leader. Maybe it’s Bret himself, based on that creepy but confusing ending grin, along with all the mentions of hallucinations and alternative versions of the truth, along with the opening game where Bret wins the “who’s the Trawler?” vote. Him as a deranged killer with multiple personalities and selective memory would fit as well as any other possibility.

Regardless, I’m afraid to say that I’m not much invested in the answer, or even in Bret’s efforts to wriggle free from his stalker. Creative new structural conceits can be fun, but what I wanted most from this penultimate episode was some basic clarification of the stakes and why any of this should matter to me, and “Hamlet” had none of that. To paraphrase Shakespeare, I bite my thumb at thee, Ryan Murphy.

Stray observations

  • • Yes, I know Murphy didn’t actually write this episode. That would be Lenore Zion, Charles Rogers, and Juli Weiner.
  • • “There’s an open space in our divorced educators book club, if you’re in.”
  • • “There’s only so many places in the world, if you think about it. Maybe 100. Like, sure, Toledo is a place, but you’re not gonna, like, go there, so for all intents and purposes it doesn’t exist.”
  • • That home invasion scene is actually very scary in the book, so it’s disappointing to see it in an abbreviated and far less suspenseful form here.
  • • I also don’t have much of a reaction to Bret and Robert hooking up. As much as I appreciate the homoeroticism on the show, I don’t think I understand either person’s real motivations here, nor does Robert’s “to be or not to be” land with any meaning.
